entry.title: Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security) [2026] ARTA 2291
entry.content:
In Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2291, the Tribunal reviewed a decision reducing Mrs Yerburgh’s age pension by assessing notional income from a farm treated as an unrealisable asset. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the rate for reassessment from 11 October 2024 on the basis that the relevant income amount was her actual annual ordinary income from the farm, not a commercial lease value.

Key holding: Where an unrealisable farm is already being worked commercially to full capacity, the amount reasonably expected from a purely commercial application under s 1130(5)(b) is the actual income from current operations, and the s 1130(5) notional rate is the lesser of that amount and 2.5% of the farm's value.

However, having heard from Mrs Yerburgh, the Tribunal is satisfied that the farm is currently being operated commercially to its full capacity. As such, the Tribunal finds that what Mrs Yerburgh could reasonably be expected to obtain from a purely commercial application of the farm is the income that is actually being generated from its current operations, not some alternative higher commercial lease figure as adopted by Centrelink.

entry.title: Fearon and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2294
entry.content:
Ms Fearon receives age pension. Centrelink treated $70,500 she effectively gifted to her daughter in December 2022 as a deprived asset. The Tribunal affirmed that decision, finding the gifting rules required the amount to be included in her assets for five years.

Key holding: A disposal of an asset, including money, for no or inadequate consideration must be included as an asset for five years from the date of disposition.

The legislation is clear, where an asset (which includes money) has been disposed of for no or inadequate consideration, it must be included as an asset for five years from the date of disposition.

entry.title: Ludlam and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security) [2026] ARTA 2445
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed Centrelink’s rejection of Ms Ludlam’s jobseeker payment claim because her combined assets exceeded the applicable limit. Centrelink treated the Cairns house as her principal home and as an asset, applying the lower homeowner assets limit. The Tribunal found Ms Ludlam was not a homeowner and remitted the claim for reassessment under the higher non-homeowner limit.

Key holding: Where a person leaves their owned home and resides in rented accommodation without an s 11A circumstance preserving it as the principal home, the person is not a homeowner under s 11(4) and the non-homeowner assets limit applies, although the former home may still be counted as an asset.

The Cairns property ceased to be Ms Ludlam's principal home when she left Cairns and took up residence in rented accommodation in Canberra. She therefore was not a homeowner as defined in subsection 11(4) of the Act and the higher asset limit applies.

entry.title: Mr Raymond Darrough v Frasers Property (APG) Pty Limited [2026] FWC 16
entry.content:
Mr Darrough lodged a general protections dismissal application under s.365 of the Fair Work Act against Frasers Property (APG) Pty Ltd outside the 21-day time limit and sought an extension of time under s.366(2). Deputy President O'Keeffe found the reason for delay (direct commercial discussions) and the merits of the claim weighed against exceptional circumstances, with the absence of prejudice and fairness considerations neutral. The application was dismissed as out of time.

Fair Work Commission, 5 Jan 2026, [2026] FWC 16

entry.title: Application by Gopal Bandameeda [2025] FWC 3842
entry.content:
Mr Bandameeda was a delivery person using Amazon's Flex app. He was deactivated after entering a customer's private residence during a delivery. The Fair Work Commission found the deactivation was unfair because serious misconduct was not established and Amazon did not comply with the Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code. The Commission ordered Amazon to reactivate his access and restore lost earnings.

Fair Work Commission, 23 Dec 2025, [2025] FWC 3842

Full text on AustLII. Not legal advice; the full text on AustLII is the authoritative version.

entry.title: Julie Saylor v Wyndham City Council [2025] FWC 3814
entry.content:
Ms Saylor lodged a general protections dismissal application against Wyndham City Council 17-20 days out of time. The Commission found no exceptional circumstances: her mental health symptoms and unfamiliarity with the 21-day limit did not provide an acceptable explanation, while the other s.366(2) factors were neutral or weighed in her favour. The application was dismissed.

Fair Work Commission, 12 Dec 2025, [2025] FWC 3814

entry.title: Mrs Penni Koroitamudu v Multhana Property Services Pty Ltd [2025] FWC 3361
entry.content:
Mrs Penni Koroitamudu lodged an unfair dismissal application against Multhana Property Services Pty Ltd. She repeatedly failed to attend a listed conference, ignored directions to file material, and did not respond to multiple opportunities to explain her non-attendance or oppose the dismissal application. The Commission dismissed the application under s399A(1)(a) and (b) for unreasonable failure to attend a conference and comply with directions.

Fair Work Commission, 7 Nov 2025, [2025] FWC 3361

entry.title: Samantha Foster v LINK-UP (N.S.W) ABORIGINAL CORPORATION [2025] FWC 2527
entry.content:
The applicant lodged an unfair dismissal application, which settled at conciliation on 1 July 2025. She later sought to reopen the matter, claiming she had not signed the terms and was coerced or lacked capacity. The Commission found a binding settlement agreement had been reached and dismissed the application under s 587 as having no reasonable prospects of success.

Fair Work Commission, 28 Aug 2025, [2025] FWC 2527

entry.title: Caruana v Darouti [2014] NSWCA 85
entry.content:
Mr George Darouti slipped and fell on a wet sloping driveway at a Seaforth property occupied by Ms Rita Caruana. The District Court entered judgment for $121,560, and the NSW Court of Appeal dismissed Ms Caruana's appeal on liability and breach issues, with no challenge to quantum.

New South Wales Court of Appeal, 28 Mar 2014, [2014] NSWCA 85
